content.rule: Used to vs. Would for Past Habits
content.explanation: We use 'used to' to talk about repeated past habits or past states that are no longer true. We use 'would' to describe repeated past actions, but NOT for past states.
content.example: She used to bake alone, and every Friday she would pipe flowers onto cupcakes.

items.notes: Transcribed from the source book; teacher verification required.

content.question: Which sentence correctly uses 'would' to describe a repeated past action?
options: She would be a famous chef five years ago.

He would have a large house when he was young.
They would like playing chess in the past.
content.correctAnswer: Every Friday, she would decorate cupcakes for fun.
content.reason: 'Would' is used for repeated past actions, but cannot be used with state verbs like 'be', 'have', or 'like'.

content.question: Why is the sentence 'He would be very shy in school' grammatically incorrect for expressing a past state?
options: 'Would' can only be used with present tense verbs.

content.passage: When Hassan taught his first free chess lesson in the corner of a youth center with a single borrowed board and six mismatched pieces, he was not thinking about legacy. He was nineteen, between university terms, and mostly hoping to fill a few empty afternoons doing something he loved instead of scrolling through his phone. Twelve children showed up that first week, mostly because a poster promised free snacks as well as the chess. Hassan later admitted that only two of them seemed genuinely interested in the game itself; the rest simply wanted somewhere to be. He kept showing up anyway, week after week, gradually learning to explain openings in language an eight-year-old could follow, and slowly the ratio shifted, until most weeks nearly the whole group asked to stay late for one more match. What Hassan noticed, almost by accident, was that teaching had begun to change the shape of his own passion. Explaining a strategy out loud, repeatedly, to children who asked blunt and occasionally brilliant questions, forced him to understand the game more deeply than years of playing alone ever had. Passion, it turned out, did not simply get passed on intact from one person to the next; it was reshaped by everyone who touched it, and Hassan’s own understanding of chess became, in a real sense, something the children had helped build. Three years later, Hassan moved to a different city for work, and the youth center asked one of his former students, by then sixteen and confident enough to run a session alone, to take over the lessons. The board is different now, and so are most of the faces around it, but the free Thursday sessions have not stopped since that first awkward afternoon with six mismatched sets. Hassan rarely mentions the club when people ask about his achievements. It never earned him any money, and his name is not officially attached to it anywhere. What he left behind, instead, is harder to put on a certificate: a room that still exists, still full most weeks, still teaching itself forward.
